prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A performance monitoring system and method is based on a Detailed Call Record (DCR). A DCR contains records of events occurring in different network domains (14, 20, 40) that are related to a single, specific VoLTE call. The DCR events for each VoLTE call cover all legs of the call, and for each call leg, the relevant events are ordered by time. A DCR also contains basic information to identify the call: the IMS Charging Identifier (ICID), the International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) of all involved subscribers, and the start and stop timestamps of the call. A DCR has all the relevant user plane measurement, radio measurement, and control plane data from all the involved domains (14, 20, 40) for all call legs of a VoLTE call, in contrast to prior art systems that focus only on a single subscriber's activities for a given call. The DCR thus provides a complete view of the call, allowing more complete analytics and troubleshooting. Furthermore, the data are collected and assembled automatically, with results available real-time, or with a few seconds delay.

outputs.L3:
A Detailed Call Record (DCR) is a comprehensive record that brings together events from multiple network domains related to one specific VoLTE call. Rather than presenting isolated information from a single network element or subscriber, a DCR consolidates all relevant data associated with the call into one unified view.

A DCR covers all legs of a VoLTE call. For each call leg, the relevant events are captured and ordered chronologically, making it possible to follow the progression of the call from setup through termination. This time-based ordering helps analysts understand how the call evolved across the different involved domains and where any issues may have occurred.

Each DCR includes basic information that uniquely identifies the call and the parties involved. This information typically includes the IMS Charging Identifier (ICID), the IMSI of each subscriber participating in the call, and the call start and stop timestamps. These identifiers allow the DCR to be correlated with other network records and used as a reliable reference for analysis, reporting, and troubleshooting.

Unlike earlier systems that were often limited to the perspective of a single subscriber, a DCR provides a broader and more complete view. It includes user plane data, radio measurement data, and control plane data from all relevant network domains and from all call legs involved in the VoLTE session. This makes it possible to analyze the full end-to-end call experience rather than only one side of the communication.

By assembling this information automatically, DCRs provide a complete and timely view of each VoLTE call. The data can be made available in real time or within seconds after the call events occur, enabling faster analytics, more effective troubleshooting, and improved understanding of network and service performance.
outputs.L4:
A performance monitoring system is configured to generate and use automatically assembled Detailed Call Records (DCRs) for voice over LTE (VoLTE) calls. Each DCR represents a comprehensive record of a specific call and is built by collecting, correlating, and ordering event information from multiple network sources. The DCR includes time-ordered event data, call and subscriber identifiers, timestamps, signaling information, and performance measurements associated with the user plane, radio access network, and control plane. It may also include information from all relevant network domains and call legs, including originating and terminating sides of the call, thereby creating a unified view of the complete end-to-end call session.

In operation, the system receives event records, signaling messages, measurements, and other network data from different elements involved in the VoLTE call. These elements may include radio access nodes, evolved packet core components, IP multimedia subsystem components, session border controllers, gateways, and other systems that participate in call setup, media transport, mobility, handover, quality management, or call release. The system correlates the received information using one or more identifiers, such as subscriber identifiers, call identifiers, session identifiers, device identifiers, bearer identifiers, IP addresses, timestamps, or other correlation keys. Once correlated, the information is assembled into a single DCR that reflects the sequence of events and performance conditions experienced during the call.

The DCR may be created in real time or near real time as the call progresses, or it may be finalized after the call ends. Because the DCR combines data across multiple layers and domains, it provides a more complete and accurate representation of call behavior than isolated records from individual network nodes. For example, the DCR can show how radio conditions, bearer establishment, signaling delays, codec negotiation, packet loss, jitter, latency, handovers, and call release causes relate to one another within the same call timeline. This allows the system to identify not only that a VoLTE call experienced degradation or failure, but also where and why the problem occurred.

Unlike earlier performance monitoring approaches that focus primarily on a single subscriber, a single network interface, or a limited set of signaling events, the DCR-based approach provides a comprehensive view of each complete VoLTE call. It captures both sides of the communication where available and correlates data from the access network, core network, IMS domain, and media transport path. As a result, the monitoring system can support deeper analytics, faster troubleshooting, and more reliable root-cause analysis.

The assembled DCRs may be used for a variety of operational and analytical purposes. Network operators can use them to detect call setup failures, dropped calls, poor voice quality, one-way audio, delayed media establishment, abnormal session releases, registration problems, mobility-related issues, and quality-of-service violations. The DCRs can also support dashboards, alarms, customer-care tools, automated diagnostics, service-level reporting, trend analysis, and machine-learning-based performance optimization. Because the information is available in real time or near real time, operators can respond more quickly to emerging network issues and can improve the overall quality and reliability of VoLTE service.

In this manner, the performance monitoring system transforms fragmented network events and measurements into a single, detailed, call-specific record. The resulting DCR enables a complete end-to-end understanding of VoLTE call performance and provides a powerful foundation for analytics, troubleshooting, and service assurance across the entire network.

A detailed call record is an important tool for keeping track of communication in a clear and organized way. It usually includes information such as the date and time of the call, the caller’s name, the phone number, the purpose of the call, key points discussed, and any follow-up actions required.

Maintaining a detailed call record helps businesses, customer service teams, and individuals stay informed and prepared. For example, if a customer calls about a service issue, the record can show what was discussed, what solution was offered, and whether further action is needed. This prevents confusion and ensures that everyone involved has access to the same information.

A good call record should be accurate, easy to read, and updated immediately after the call. It can improve communication, support better decision-making, and provide a reliable history of interactions. Whether used in sales, support, healthcare, or administration, detailed call records play a key role in professional and efficient communication.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how a Detailed Call Record improves VoLTE troubleshooting compared with prior art systems that only monitor one subscriber’s call activity.
counterfactuals.output:
A Detailed Call Record (DCR) improves VoLTE troubleshooting because it gives a more complete, end-to-end view of the VoLTE session rather than only showing activity associated with one monitored subscriber.

Compared with prior systems that track only one subscriber’s call activity, a DCR can improve troubleshooting in several ways:

1. **End-to-end call visibility**  
   A VoLTE call involves both the originating and terminating parties, IMS signaling, LTE bearers, policy control, and often multiple network nodes. A DCR can capture details for the whole call flow, not just the events seen from one subscriber’s side.

2. **Correlation of both call legs**  
   If only one subscriber is monitored, failures on the far-end leg may be invisible. A DCR can correlate the originating and terminating legs, helping determine whether a problem occurred with the caller, the callee, or somewhere in between.

3. **Better failure localization**  
   VoLTE problems can be caused by radio issues, IMS registration problems, SIP signaling failures, bearer setup failures, codec negotiation issues, or handover problems. A DCR can include enough information to identify which portion of the network or procedure failed.

4. **Richer signaling and session information**  
   A DCR may include SIP messages, response codes, timestamps, call setup events, termination causes, device identifiers, cell information, bearer/QoS details, and media-related parameters. This gives engineers more context than a simple subscriber activity log.

5. **Improved timing analysis**  
   Because VoLTE troubleshooting often depends on the sequence and timing of events, a DCR can show when each major event occurred. This helps detect delays in call setup, bearer creation, registration, routing, or call release.

6. **Detection of issues invisible to one-sided monitoring**  
   A subscriber-only view may show that a call failed, dropped, or had poor quality, but not why. The cause may be on the terminating side, in IMS routing, in interconnect, or in a network element not directly associated with the monitored subscriber. A DCR helps expose those hidden causes.

7. **Reduced need for manual log correlation**  
   Without a DCR, engineers may need to collect separate logs from multiple systems and manually match them using timestamps, phone numbers, IMS identifiers, or session IDs. A DCR can consolidate or correlate this information, speeding diagnosis.

8. **More accurate root-cause analysis**  
   By combining subscriber, network, signaling, and session information, a DCR helps distinguish between symptoms and causes. For example, it can help determine whether a failed VoLTE call was due to radio coverage, IMS rejection, policy/QoS failure, unavailable terminating user, or abnormal release.

In short, prior art systems that monitor only one subscriber provide a partial, one-sided view of a VoLTE call. A Detailed Call Record improves troubleshooting by creating a correlated, detailed, end-to-end record of the VoLTE session, allowing faster and more accurate identification of where and why a call problem occurred.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In technical terms, describe a real-time VoLTE performance monitoring approach based on assembling events from domains 14, 20, and 40 into a unified DCR for each call.
counterfactuals.output:
A real-time VoLTE performance monitoring approach can be implemented by correlating protocol/event feeds from domains **14, 20, and 40** into a single unified **Detailed Call Record, DCR**, for each VoLTE call session. The objective is to reconstruct the end-to-end call lifecycle across radio, packet-core/IMS, and service/session domains, then compute call-level KPIs in near real time.

## 1. Event acquisition from domains 14, 20, and 40

Each domain produces time-stamped signaling and/or user-plane performance events related to the same VoLTE call.

Typical event sources may include:

- **Domain 14**: access/RAN or bearer-related events  
  Examples: LTE attach context, EPS bearer setup, dedicated bearer activation, handover, radio release, QCI/ARP information, RRC events.

- **Domain 20**: EPC/packet-core events  
  Examples: MME, SGW, PGW, PCRF interactions, GTP-C session creation/modification/deletion, IMS APN bearer handling, QCI 1 bearer establishment, policy charging events.

- **Domain 40**: IMS/SIP/service-layer events  
  Examples: SIP `INVITE`, `100 Trying`, `180 Ringing`, `183 Session Progress`, `200 OK`, `ACK`, `BYE`, `CANCEL`, `4xx/5xx/6xx` responses, TAS/S-CSCF/P-CSCF events, RTP/RTCP quality indicators.

The monitoring system ingests these feeds in real time using probes, mediation systems, message buses, or streaming collectors.

## 2. Normalization into a common event model

Because each domain has different protocol formats and identifiers, incoming records are normalized into a canonical internal schema.

A normalized event may contain:

```text
event_time
ingest_time
domain_id
network_element
protocol
procedure_type
event_type
subscriber_id
imsi
msisdn
imei
sip_call_id
sip_from_tag
sip_to_tag
pani / visited-network-id
ip_address
ue_ip
apn
bearer_id
ebi
qci
teid
cell_id
tac
cause_code
result_code
direction
raw_reference
```

Normalization is critical because domain 14, 20, and 40 may refer to the same call using different identifiers. For example:

- IMS/SIP uses `Call-ID`, `From tag`, `To tag`, SIP URI, IMPU/IMPI.
- EPC uses IMSI, MSISDN, UE IP, APN, EBI, TEID.
- RAN/access events use IMSI, GUTI, cell ID, bearer ID, or radio connection identifiers.

## 3. Cross-domain correlation

The system correlates events into one call context using deterministic and probabilistic keys.

Common correlation keys include:

```text
SIP Call-ID
IMSI
MSISDN
IMPU / SIP URI
UE IP address
EPS bearer ID, especially QCI 1 bearer
TEID
APN, usually IMS APN
cell ID / TAC
event timestamp proximity
SIP dialog tuple: Call-ID + From tag + To tag
```

A correlation engine maintains an in-memory state object for each active call. As events arrive from domains 14, 20, and 40, they are attached to the matching call context.

Example correlation flow:

1. SIP `INVITE` from domain 40 creates a provisional call context.
2. IMS identifiers are extracted: SIP `Call-ID`, calling party, called party, P-CSCF, S-CSCF, TAS.
3. The UE IP or IMSI is used to associate the SIP session with EPC bearer events from domain 20.
4. QCI 1 dedicated bearer activation from domain 20 is linked to the same call.
5. Radio/access events from domain 14 are attached using IMSI, bearer ID, cell ID, and timestamp alignment.
6. SIP answer, failure, or release events complete the call signaling timeline.
7. RTP/RTCP or bearer quality events are merged to add media-quality metrics.

## 4. Unified DCR construction

The unified DCR represents the full VoLTE call lifecycle, not just one interface or protocol leg.

A DCR may include:

```text
dcr_id
call_start_time
call_end_time
call_duration
calling_party
called_party
imsi
msisdn
imei
ue_ip
sip_call_id
call_direction
originating_network
terminating_network
roaming_status
access_type
cell_id_start
cell_id_end
tac
ims_apn
qci
bearer_establishment_time
sip_invite_time
sip_180_time
sip_183_time
sip_200ok_time
sip_ack_time
sip_bye_time
release_cause
failure_cause
drop_cause
handover_count
radio_failures
packet_core_failures
ims_failures
rtp_packet_loss
jitter
latency
mos
domain_14_event_refs
domain_20_event_refs
domain_40_event_refs
```

The DCR is continuously enriched as more events arrive. It can be emitted in several stages:

- **Partial DCR** when the call is detected.
- **Updated DCR** as bearer, SIP, and media events arrive.
- **Final DCR** when the call is released or when an inactivity timeout occurs.

## 5. Stateful call reconstruction

The system typically uses a call-state machine. Example states:

```text
IDLE
CALL_ATTEMPTED
IMS_INVITE_SEEN
DEDICATED_BEARER_REQUESTED
DEDICATED_BEARER_ESTABLISHED
RINGING
ANSWERED
MEDIA_ACTIVE
RELEASING
COMPLETED
FAILED
DROPPED
```

Transitions are triggered by domain events.

For example:

```text
SIP INVITE               -> CALL_ATTEMPTED
GTP Create Bearer        -> DEDICATED_BEARER_REQUESTED
Bearer activation OK     -> DEDICATED_BEARER_ESTABLISHED
SIP 180/183              -> RINGING
SIP 200 OK + ACK         -> ANSWERED / MEDIA_ACTIVE
SIP BYE                  -> RELEASING
Bearer deletion          -> COMPLETED
Radio loss or abnormal release -> DROPPED
SIP 4xx/5xx/6xx          -> FAILED
```

This stateful model allows the monitoring system to distinguish between:

- normal call completion,
- setup failure,
- post-answer drop,
- bearer establishment failure,
- IMS signaling failure,
- access/RAN failure,
- packet-core policy or bearer failure.

## 6. KPI calculation

Once events are assembled into a unified DCR, call-level KPIs can be calculated in real time.

Common VoLTE KPIs include:

### Accessibility KPIs

```text
Call setup success rate, CSSR
VoLTE registration success rate
Dedicated bearer setup success rate
IMS session setup success rate
```

### Retainability KPIs

```text
Call drop rate
Abnormal release rate
Dedicated bearer loss rate
Radio-induced call drop rate
```

### Setup-time KPIs

```text
Post-dial delay, PDD
SIP INVITE-to-180 time
SIP INVITE-to-183 time
SIP INVITE-to-200 OK time
Bearer establishment latency
IMS call setup latency
```

### Media-quality KPIs

```text
RTP packet loss
Jitter
Round-trip delay
MOS / R-factor
Codec used, e.g. AMR-WB or EVS
One-way audio indicators
Silence or RTP gap duration
```

### Mobility KPIs

```text
Handover count during call
SRVCC attempt/success/failure
Cell-level drop correlation
Tracking-area or eNodeB failure concentration
```

## 7. Real-time processing architecture

A typical implementation uses a streaming architecture:

```text
Domain probes / collectors
        ↓
Protocol decoders
        ↓
Event normalization
        ↓
Message bus, e.g. Kafka
        ↓
Stream correlation engine
        ↓
In-memory call session store
        ↓
DCR generation
        ↓
KPI engine / alerting / dashboards / data lake
```

The correlation engine may be implemented using stream-processing frameworks such as Flink, Spark Structured Streaming, Kafka Streams, or a custom low-latency stateful processor.

Important design aspects include:

- event-time processing rather than only ingest-time processing,
- tolerance for out-of-order events,
- configurable correlation windows,
- late-event handling,
- duplicate suppression,
- clock synchronization between probes,
- high-cardinality session indexing,
- timeout-based DCR closure,
- enrichment using subscriber, cell, and topology databases.

## 8. Handling out-of-order and missing events

In live networks, events from domains 14, 20, and 40 may arrive with different delays. The DCR builder should therefore support:

- buffering windows,
- late-arrival updates,
- confidence scoring for correlation,
- partial DCR generation,
- re-opening or amending recently closed DCRs,
- default cause mapping when one domain is missing.

For example, if the SIP `BYE` is missing but the QCI 1 bearer deletion and radio release are observed, the system can infer call termination and close the DCR with an inferred release type.

## 9. Cause-code normalization

Different domains report failures differently. The system maps them into a common cause taxonomy.

Example:

```text
IMS failure:
  SIP 403, 404, 408, 480, 486, 500, 503

EPC failure:
  GTP cause: request rejected, no resources, APN restriction, bearer failure
  Diameter Rx/Gx failure: policy rejection, authorization failure

RAN/access failure:
  radio link failure
  handover failure
  RRC abnormal release
  coverage loss
```

The unified DCR should contain both:

```text
raw_cause_code
normalized_cause_category
responsible_domain
probable_root_cause
```

This allows service assurance teams to determine whether a failed or dropped VoLTE call was caused by IMS, packet core, policy control, transport, or radio conditions.

## 10. Result

The result is a real-time, end-to-end VoLTE call record that combines the signaling, bearer, radio, and media context of a single call.

Instead of analyzing isolated records from domains 14, 20, and 40, the operator obtains one unified DCR per call, enabling:

- end-to-end call trace reconstruction,
- real-time VoLTE KPI reporting,
- rapid failure localization,
- subscriber-level troubleshooting,
- cell and network-element impact analysis,
- proactive alarming on degradation,
- accurate customer-experience monitoring.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
